title: 'An exciting event:' Dark matter or not, new SURF discovery marks potential breakthrough
excerpt: "It isn't anything else that we know of, so either way, we probably discovered a novel particle."
content:
LEAD-DEADWOOD — While scientists at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) won’t say they’ve definitely discovered dark matter, they’re still calling it an “exciting event.”

On Thursday, Sept. 10, Julia Delgaudio, engineering specialist for SURF’s LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, met with members of the public at the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor Center for the latest edition of its Ask a Scientist program. Fifteen people attended the discussion, which centered on LZ’s recent observation of what officials are calling "something entirely unique."

"It isn't anything else that we know of, so either way, we probably discovered a novel particle," Delgaudio told the crowd.

Delgaudio said significantly more analysis will be done before hard conclusions are drawn, yet the event still represents a potential breakthrough for the LZ team.

On Sept. 1, SURF announced that LZ recorded a single particle interaction that thus far defies explanation. SURF emphasized that while the result doesn’t meet the threshold for an official discovery, it is the most compelling hint of dark matter reported by the experiment to date.

"We found a promising event that we can't say isn't dark matter, but we're reluctant to say it is dark matter because it's just one event," Delgaudio said.

The LZ experiment is an international effort between 250 scientists and engineers. Located 4,850 feet underground in the remnants of the Homestake Mine, it utilizes 10 metric tonnes of ultrapure liquid xenon to search for evidence of dark matter. It is specifically optimized to look for WIMPs, or weakly interacting massive particles, one of the leading candidates in solving the dark matter mystery.

Delgaudio explained that, per mathematical models, between 75%-85% of the universe is composed of invisible “dark matter.” When asked how confident officials are about this, Delgaudio responded that, simply put, the math doesn’t align without it.

"The universe moves in ways that means there's more gravity than we can account for with the matter that we can detect," she said.

The goal of LZ, as well as its predecessor LUX, is to identify tangible data on this elusive substance. Delgaudio said that dark matter’s definitive discovery will revolutionize the understanding of science, and in particular, the perceived expansion of the universe.

"We're pretty sure that dark matter drives that expansion. We don't know. We think it does, and so, if we can figure out what it is, where it comes from, then we will be a lot closer to answering, ‘Does it end?’" Delgaudio noted.

Delgaudio also explained how this observation will aid in adjusting the experiment for future tests, adding that it may have given credence to a previously fringe theory. She described how some experimental physicists believe there could be seasonal oscillations in the amount of dark matter concentrated on Earth’s surface, with summer months potentially seeing larger quantities.

The breakthrough observation lines up with this conjecture. Due to the availability of student scientists, much of the experiment’s calibration work is conducted in the summer, yet this is now being reconsidered.

"We're rethinking that a lot right now because when we're calibrating, we're not collecting data,” Delgaudio said.

The LZ team had ended their calibration work for the day only 90 minutes prior to the particle event.

Delgaudio noted how it's a testament to the thoroughness of research that it took the team three years to come out with "a maybe" in regard to the dark matter question.

When it was first observed, she said, the initial reaction was that the event was likely the result of salting, a process where fake events are placed into the data set to test whether students will catch them.

"The group that found this (one of the smaller LZ teams) was never actually expected to find dark matter. They were filtering out events that they were keyed in to filter out," Delgaudio explained. “They found one that didn't filter out.”

The rest of the scientific community is still processing the announcement, Delgaudio said, and it will take time before anything concrete emerges. In the meantime, scientists from around the world will be looking closely at the event to work out exactly what took place and what can be learned from it.

To Delgaudio, this collaboration is paramount to scientific discovery.

"That's the fun part about physics. You really go, 'I think I discovered something. Who wants to check my notes?'" she said.
